unit.title: Plan and apply time management strategies

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Why is good time management important at work?
options: It means you never have to work with other people
It lets you skip the safety checks to save time
It means your supervisor never checks your work
It helps you do good work on time with less rush

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of poor time management?
options: Jobs are finished by the time agreed
Tools are put back in the same place each day
The worker writes a list of tasks each morning
The worker often rushes and misses deadlines

questions.stem: Being on time for work helps the team because:
options: work can start as planned and others are not held up
the worker can leave early without telling anyone
the supervisor no longer needs to plan the day
the worker gets paid extra for each minute early

questions.stem: Before planning the day, where should a worker first find out what jobs must be done?
options: From a friend who works at another company
From what they remember of last month's jobs
From the jobs they enjoy doing the most
From the supervisor, job sheets or work orders

questions.stem: Andre is given a job but is not sure when it must be finished. What should he do?
options: Guess a date and hope that it is right
Leave it until someone asks him about it
Do it last, after all of his other work
Ask the supervisor for the deadline

questions.stem: What is a deadline?
options: The time or date by which a job must be done
The time a worker has lunch each day
A line painted on the floor by a machine
The last day of the month when pay comes

questions.stem: A villa supervisor says, "Rooms 1 to 4 must be ready by 3 pm, as guests arrive then." What does this tell the housekeeper?
options: The time limit for the job and why it matters
That the guests will clean the rooms themselves
That the rooms can be finished tomorrow
That only one room needs to be cleaned today

questions.stem: What does it mean to "prioritise" your tasks?
options: To do the easiest tasks first and leave the rest
To do all your tasks at exactly the same time
To give your tasks to someone else to do
To put tasks in order of how much they matter

questions.stem: Which of these tasks should usually come first?
options: Fixing a broken step that guests or workers use
Painting the office walls a new colour next month
Sorting old magazines in the staff room
Planning the staff party for December

questions.stem: A task that is both urgent and important should be:
options: left until the end of the week
done straight away
given to a customer to do
written down and forgotten

questions.stem: A task is important but not urgent, such as planning next month's machine maintenance. What should you do with it?
options: Ignore it, because nobody needs it done today
Plan a set time to do it before it becomes urgent
Drop everything else you are doing and do it now
Wait until it turns into an emergency

questions.stem: Kemar has three jobs: weld a gate due tomorrow, tidy the tool cupboard, and sort scrap for next week's collection. Which should he do first?
options: Sort the scrap, because it is the easiest
Tidy the cupboard, because it takes the least time
Do all three a little at a time
Weld the gate, because it is due soonest

questions.stem: Tashana is cleaning a villa room when a guest reports water leaking onto the hallway floor. What should she do?
options: Make the area safe and report it, as it is a hazard
Finish cleaning the room first, then look at the leak
Tell the guest to call back after her lunch break
Write it on her list for tomorrow's jobs

questions.stem: Which tool helps you sort tasks into "urgent" and "important"?
options: A tape measure
A shopping receipt
A priority grid with four boxes
A list of the staff's phone numbers

questions.stem: Two jobs are due at the same time and you cannot do both. What should you do?
options: Do the one you like best and hope for the best
Do neither, as both cannot be done anyway
Tell the supervisor early and agree the order
Do both quickly, skipping the safety checks

questions.stem: Why should safety jobs, such as checking a gas hose for leaks before use, never be skipped to save time?
options: Because they are the quickest jobs of the day
Because the supervisor likes to check them later on
Because they can be done after the job instead
Because skipping them can cause injury or damage

questions.stem: What is a to-do list?
options: A list of jobs you have already been paid for
A list of people you do not want to work with
A list of tasks you need to do, often in order
A list of tools that are broken in the workshop

questions.stem: Why is it useful to tick off tasks on a list as you finish them?
options: It makes the list shorter to print
You can see what is done and what is still left
It tells the supervisor you need a pay rise
It stops anyone else adding jobs to the list

questions.stem: Marsha has meetings, deliveries and staff days off to keep track of for the whole month. Which tool suits this best?
options: A calendar or wall planner
A sticky note on her phone
Her memory of last year's plan
A receipt book

questions.stem: What does a work schedule show?
options: How much each worker is paid every week
Which tasks are done, by whom and when
The phone numbers of all the customers
The rules for using the staff car park

questions.stem: A chart that shows each task as a bar along a timeline, so you can see when each one starts and ends, is called a:
options: Pie chart
Gantt chart
Flow chart
Seating chart

questions.stem: How can a mobile phone help with time management at work?
options: By playing music to make the day pass quicker
By letting you chat to friends while you work
By setting reminders and alarms for tasks
By taking selfies to show you are at work

questions.stem: When you work out how long a job will take, what should you include?
options: Only the time spent actually welding or cleaning
Only the time your best friend would need
Only the time shown on last year's price list
Set-up, the work itself, checking and clean-up

questions.stem: What is a SMART goal?
options: A goal that is clear, measurable and has a time limit
A goal that only very clever people are able to reach
A goal that is kept secret from the supervisor and team
A goal that changes every day without a plan

questions.stem: Which of these is a SMART goal?
options: I will try to be a bit faster at my work
I will work harder some time in the next while
I will cut and tack 6 frames by 12 noon today
I will be the very best worker the company has

questions.stem: Why should a big job, such as making a security grille, be broken into smaller steps?
options: So that it looks like a lot more work than it really is
So that the customer pays for each step
So each step can be planned, timed and checked
So that the job can be left half finished

questions.stem: Why is it wise to add a little extra time when you plan a job?
options: To allow for delays you did not expect
So you can take a longer lunch break
So the customer pays a higher price
To make the plan look much neater on paper

questions.stem: Delroy thought a job would take 2 hours, but it took 4. What should he do next time he plans a similar job?
options: Plan 2 hours again and work faster
Stop planning, as plans never work
Use what he learned to plan more time
Blame the tools and not change anything

questions.stem: Which of these is a common time waster in a workshop?
options: Searching for tools that were not put back
Checking the machine before starting work
Reading the drawing before cutting steel
Putting on the right PPE before the job starts

questions.stem: What is procrastination?
options: Doing tasks in the right order
Putting off a task you should do now
Finishing a job before the deadline
Asking for help when you are stuck

questions.stem: Ricardo keeps putting off writing his job report because he does not like it. What is the best way to deal with this?
options: Wait until he feels like writing it
Set a short, fixed time to start it now
Ask a friend to write it for him
Leave it out, as reports do not matter

questions.stem: How does a tidy, well-organised work area save time?
options: It means the area never has to be cleaned again
It means you can skip the safety checks
It means the supervisor will not visit
It means tools and materials are quick to find

questions.stem: A co-worker keeps stopping by to chat while Kimone is trying to finish a booking report. What is the best thing to do?
options: Chat for as long as they want, to be friendly
Tell them rudely to go away and to leave her alone
Politely say she is busy and offer to talk at break
Stop the report and go home early

questions.stem: Which is the best way to handle personal phone calls and messages during work time?
options: Answer every one at once, wherever you are
Keep them for breaks unless there is an emergency
Answer them while running a machine to save time
Turn the phone up loud so you never miss one

questions.stem: Shanice checks her phone every few minutes while working. What is the likely result?
options: She finishes all her work much faster than usual
She makes fewer mistakes than usual
Her work takes longer and has more mistakes
Her supervisor gives her more free time

questions.stem: Which of these is an unplanned interruption?
options: The morning team meeting at 7:30 am every day
The lunch break taken at the same time each day
A machine breaking down in the middle of a job
A weekly cleaning task that is on the roster

questions.stem: Your supervisor gives you a new job when you already have a full day. What should you do?
options: Explain your other tasks and ask which comes first
Say yes and then leave one job without telling anyone
Refuse the job and walk away
Do the new job badly so you are not asked again

questions.stem: When is a good time to plan the next day's tasks?
options: At the end of today, before you go home
Only after the supervisor shouts at you
In the middle of a weld or a cleaning job
Never, as each day plans itself

questions.stem: How can working well as a team save time on a job?
options: Each person can do the same task over again
Nobody needs to know what the others are doing
Tasks are shared and people help each other
Everyone can take a break at the same time

questions.stem: Odane needs a grinder that another worker is using. What is the best way to plan for this?
options: Take it while the other worker is away on break
Wait and do nothing until it becomes free
Use a damaged grinder from the scrap bin
Agree a time to use it and do other work first

questions.stem: Why should you write down instructions when a supervisor gives you several jobs at once?
options: To show the supervisor you have good handwriting
So you do not forget a job or a detail
So you can give the list to a customer
To make the instructions take longer

questions.stem: A job card says the delivery will arrive at 14:30. What time is this?
Your shift starts at 7:00 am. The bus takes 45 minutes and you need 15 minutes to change into work clothes. What is the latest bus you should catch?
What is a time log?
options: A piece of wood used to prop open a door
A clock fixed to the wall of the workshop
A record of what you did and how long it took
A list of the shop's opening times

questions.stem: At the end of the week, Jermaine compares his plan with what he really did. Why is this useful?
options: It proves he was right all along
It shows him how to plan better next time
It means he needs no plan next week
It gives him a reason to blame others

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: How do you write 5:00 pm in the 24-hour clock?
What do we call a regular, set order of tasks that you follow every day, such as the checks at the start of a shift?
What is a common name for the short meeting at the start of a shift where the team talks about the day's work and safety?
What do we call a written list of checks or steps that you go through and tick, so that nothing is missed?
A job must be finished by the end of Friday and needs 3 full working days. It is now Monday morning. On which day must you start, at the latest?
What do we call handing a task to another suitable person to do, while you stay responsible for it being done?
What is the name of the chart, often on the wall, that shows which staff work which shifts each week?
How many minutes are there in 2.5 hours?
What one word describes the habit of arriving at work and at meetings on time?
A shift runs from 07:00 to 15:30 with a 30-minute lunch break. How many hours are worked?
What do we call trying to do two or more tasks at the same time?
What do we call time when a machine or a worker cannot work because of a breakdown or waiting for materials?
What do we call the list of points to be discussed at a meeting, sent out before it starts?
In a project plan, what do we call a key point that marks the end of a main stage, such as "frame welded"?
A job is planned to take 90 minutes and starts at 10:45 am. At what time should it finish?

essays.stem: Explain why good time management is important for a worker and for the business. Give examples from a workshop or a villa.
essays.modelAnswer: Good time management means planning work so that the right jobs are done well and on time. For the worker it lowers stress, because there is less rushing at the end of the day, and fewer mistakes are made. It also builds a good name, which can lead to more responsibility and better pay. For the business, jobs finished on time keep customers happy and bring repeat work. In a workshop, if a gate is promised for Friday and is late, the customer may go somewhere else, and the business loses money on wasted labour. Good planning also means safety checks are not skipped in a rush. In a villa, rooms must be clean and ready before guests check in. If they are late, guests wait, complain and may post a bad review. Good time management also means tools, machines and staff are used well, so costs stay down.
markingPoints: Says what good time management is: the right jobs done well and on time
Benefit to the worker: less stress, fewer mistakes, a good name
Benefit to the business: happy customers, repeat work, lower costs
Suitable workshop example (late job, safety checks not skipped)
Suitable villa example (rooms ready before check-in)

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan your tasks for a working day, from getting your instructions to the end of the shift.
essays.modelAnswer: At the start of the day I get my instructions from the supervisor, the job sheets or the roster, and make sure I know each deadline. I write all the tasks on a to-do list. Then I put them in order: safety and urgent jobs first, then jobs with the nearest deadlines, then the rest. I estimate how long each task will take, including fetching tools and materials, setting up, checking and cleaning up, and I add a little extra time for delays. I check that the tools, machines and materials I need will be free when I need them. I plan my breaks. During the day I work through the list, tick off each task, and tell the supervisor at once if something will be late. At the end of the shift I clean up, report what is done and what is left, and plan the next day.
markingPoints: Gets instructions and deadlines from the supervisor, job sheets or roster
Lists the tasks and puts them in priority order
Estimates time, including set-up and clean-up, with extra time for delays
Checks that tools, machines and materials are available
Works through and ticks off tasks, reports delays, and reviews at the end of the shift

essays.stem: Explain how to use an urgent and important grid to sort tasks. Give an example of a task for each of the four boxes.
essays.modelAnswer: The grid has four boxes made by asking two questions about each task. Is it urgent, meaning it must be done soon? Is it important, meaning it matters a lot for safety, customers or the business? Box 1 is urgent and important, so I do it now. An example is reporting a smell of gas in the workshop, or helping a guest who is locked out of a room. Box 2 is important but not urgent, so I plan a set time for it. An example is weekly maintenance of the welding machines or a deep clean of the villa kitchen. Box 3 is urgent but not important, so I deal with it quickly or pass it to the right person. An example is a sales call wanting an answer today. Box 4 is neither urgent nor important, so I do it last or drop it, such as browsing social media. The grid helps me spend my time on what matters most.
markingPoints: Explains the two questions: urgent (soon) and important (matters a lot)
Urgent and important: do now, with a suitable example
Important, not urgent: plan a time, with a suitable example
Urgent, not important: deal with quickly or pass on, with a suitable example
Neither: do last or drop, with a suitable example

essays.stem: Describe five common time wasters at work and say how each one can be reduced.
essays.modelAnswer: The first is looking for tools and materials. This is reduced by keeping the work area tidy, returning tools to a labelled place or shadow board, and storing stock in order. The second is personal phone use and social media. The phone can be kept in a locker or bag and used only on breaks. The third is unplanned chats and visitors. I can politely say I am busy and offer to talk at the break. The fourth is putting off tasks I do not like. I can break the task into small steps and start with a short, fixed time, such as ten minutes. The fifth is redoing work because instructions were not clear. I should ask questions, read the drawing or the job sheet and check measurements before starting. Another time waster is waiting for machines or materials, which can be reduced by booking shared machines and ordering stock early.
markingPoints: Looking for tools or materials, reduced by tidy, labelled storage
Personal phone or social media use, reduced by keeping it for breaks
Unplanned chats or visitors, handled politely
Putting off tasks, reduced by small steps and a fixed start time
Redoing work or waiting for resources, reduced by checking instructions or planning ahead

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the time needed for a job, such as making and painting a small steel gate, and why you should check the estimate afterwards.
essays.modelAnswer: First I break the job into steps. For a small steel gate these are: read the drawing and list the materials, collect and check the steel, mark out and cut the pieces, tack the frame and check it is square, weld it out, grind and clean, prime and paint, let the paint dry, and clean up. For each step I think how long it takes, using what I or the supervisor know from earlier jobs. I include time to fetch materials, set up machines and PPE, check the work and clean up, not just the cutting and welding. I add the steps together and add some extra time for delays, such as a power cut or waiting for a grinder. I write the estimate down and plan with it. Afterwards I compare the real time with my estimate. If it took longer, I find out why and use this to make better estimates, so customers are given dates that can be kept.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into steps
Estimates each step from experience or by asking the supervisor
Includes fetching, set-up, checking, drying and clean-up time
Adds extra time for delays
Compares the real time afterwards and uses it to improve future estimates

essays.stem: Explain what you should do when you realise that you cannot finish a job by its deadline.
essays.modelAnswer: As soon as I see that the job will be late, I tell my supervisor. I do not wait until the deadline has passed. I explain the reason clearly and honestly, for example the steel delivery is late, a machine broke down, or more rooms need cleaning than planned. I say how much is done and how much is left, and give a realistic new time. I suggest ways to help, such as getting a co-worker to assist, working on another part of the job while I wait, or finishing the most important part first. I do not rush in an unsafe way or skip safety and quality checks to save time, because this can cause injury, or poor work that must be done again. If the supervisor agrees, the customer or guest is told politely and given the new time. Afterwards I note what caused the delay so that it can be planned for next time.
markingPoints: Tells the supervisor as soon as the delay is known
Explains the reason, the progress so far and a realistic new time
Suggests solutions such as help from others or changing the order of work
Does not skip safety or quality checks to catch up
Customer told politely; the cause is noted for next time

essays.stem: Compare a to-do list, a calendar or wall planner, and a Gantt chart as planning tools. Say what each one is best used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A to-do list is a simple list of tasks for the day or the week, often in order of priority. It is quick to write and easy to tick off, so it is best for one person's daily jobs. But it does not show times or who does what. A calendar or wall planner shows days and dates, so it is best for fixed events over weeks or months, such as meetings, deliveries, guest arrivals, staff days off and deadlines. Everyone can see it on the wall or on a shared phone calendar. A Gantt chart shows each task as a bar along a timeline, with its start and finish, and often who does it. It is best for a bigger job with many steps that follow each other, such as making and fitting a stair rail, because it shows which steps must finish before others start and whether the job is on time. Many workplaces use all three together.
markingPoints: To-do list: simple list of tasks, best for daily jobs; does not show times or people
Calendar or wall planner: shows dates, best for fixed events and deadlines over weeks or months
Gantt chart: tasks as bars on a timeline, best for bigger jobs with steps in order
Fair comparison of a strength or weakness, or the point that they can be used together

essays.stem: Describe how to set a SMART goal, using an example from your own training or trade.
essays.modelAnswer: A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. Specific means it says clearly what I will do. Measurable means I can count or check it, so I know when it is done. Achievable means it is possible with my skills, tools and time. Relevant means it matters to my job or training. Time-bound means it has a deadline. A goal like "I want to get better at welding" is not SMART. A SMART version is: "By the end of this month I will weld five fillet joints in the horizontal position that pass my instructor's visual check." This says what (fillet joints), how many (five), how it is checked (the instructor's check), why it matters (it is part of my qualification) and when (the end of the month). A villa trainee might set: "By Friday I will clean and make up a guest room to standard in 30 minutes."
markingPoints: Names the five parts: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound
Explains what each part means
Shows a goal that is not SMART and how to improve it
Gives a SMART example with a clear measure and a deadline
Example is linked to the trainee's own training or trade

essays.stem: Explain how taking proper breaks and looking after your health help you to manage your time, and describe signs that a worker's workload is too heavy.
essays.modelAnswer: A tired worker works slowly and makes more mistakes, and mistakes take time to fix. Short breaks, drinking water and eating properly keep energy up, especially in a hot workshop or when cleaning many rooms in the heat. Enough sleep means a worker arrives on time and alert. In welding and machine work, a tired worker is more likely to have an accident, which costs far more time than a break. Signs that a workload is too heavy include always working through breaks, often staying late, missing deadlines, feeling stressed or unable to sleep, making more mistakes than usual, getting headaches, and being short-tempered with others. If these signs appear, the worker should plan and prioritise again, ask for help, and talk to the supervisor about the workload before it causes harm.
markingPoints: Tired workers are slower and make more mistakes
Breaks, water, food and sleep keep energy up, especially in the heat
Tiredness raises the risk of accidents
At least two signs of a heavy workload
Action: re-plan, ask for help and talk to the supervisor

essays.stem: Describe how you would keep a time log for one week, and how you would use it to improve the way you manage your time.
essays.modelAnswer: A time log is a record of how I really spend my time. For one week I would use a notebook or a sheet with columns for the time, what I was doing, and notes. Every 30 minutes, or each time I change task, I write down what I did, for example "08:00–08:40 cutting steel for gate frame" or "10:15–10:30 looking for the grinder". I write honestly, including breaks, interruptions and phone use. At the end of the week I add up the time spent on each kind of activity. I compare this with my plan to see where time was lost, such as searching for tools, waiting for materials or chatting. I then choose two or three changes, like returning tools to the shadow board, ordering materials earlier, or keeping my phone in my locker. I talk about the log with my supervisor, try the changes the next week, and check again to see if they worked.
markingPoints: Explains that a time log records how time is really spent
Records time, task and notes often and honestly, including interruptions
Totals the time and compares it with the plan
Finds the time wasters and chooses changes
Tries the changes, reviews again and discusses with the supervisor

practical1.title: Plan a week's work for a team from a job list
practical1.brief: As a group, plan a five-day work schedule for a small team. The assessor gives you one scenario card: a fabrication shop (for example a gate due Thursday, burglar bars for three windows due Friday, an urgent trailer repair, a consumables order, machine maintenance and booth cleaning, with one bandsaw and two welding machines to share), or a villa (for example guest arrivals and departures, a deep clean, laundry, a supplies order, the pool area and a staff day off). Work in these stages, and give each member at least one stage to lead while the others help: (1) write every task and its deadline on a sticky note; (2) sort the notes on an urgent and important grid on chart paper; (3) estimate the time for each task, including set-up, safety checks, clean-up and some extra time; (4) draw a Monday-to-Friday schedule or Gantt chart showing who does what and when, with no clashes on shared machines or staff; (5) present the plan to the assessor, who acts as the supervisor, with each member explaining one part and answering questions. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A scenario card from the assessor (fabrication shop or villa)
Sticky notes, markers and chart paper
A ruler for drawing the schedule
A blank weekly planner or Gantt chart sheet
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: All the tasks and deadlines written on sticky notes
The urgent and important grid with every task placed
The table of time estimates for each task
The finished Monday-to-Friday schedule or Gantt chart
The group presenting the plan to the assessor
The final plan with any changes the assessor asked for
checklist: Found every task and deadline on the scenario card
Placed tasks in the grid correctly and gave a reason
Gave realistic time estimates, including set-up, safety checks, clean-up and extra time
Kept safety checks and maintenance in the plan instead of dropping them
Shared out tasks fairly with no clashes on machines, rooms or staff
Wrote times and days clearly and correctly
Explained their part of the plan clearly and answered the assessor's questions
Listened to others and took a full part in the group
safety: Plan time for PPE, safety checks and clean-up in every job; never plan them out to save time
Do not plan anyone to use a machine they are not trained or allowed to use
Plan proper breaks and water in hot conditions; do not plan anyone to work long hours without rest
Keep the work room tidy, with bags and chairs out of the walkways

practical2.title: Role play: re-plan a working day when interruptions happen
practical2.brief: As a group, work through a planned day in timed rounds. The assessor gives you a schedule for one day at a fabrication shop or a villa, written on chart paper, and each round of 15 minutes stands for one hour of the working day. During the rounds the assessor hands out interruption cards, for example a welding machine breaks down, steel is delivered late, a worker calls in sick, a guest checks in early, or a customer phones wanting a job sooner. Each member leads the group's answer to at least one card: decide the new priority, change the schedule on the chart paper, and role-play telling the supervisor or customer (played by the assessor) about any changed time, politely and early. Every member also keeps a simple time log of what they do during the session. At the end, the group fills in a review sheet: what was planned, what really happened, what wasted time, and what you would do differently. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A one-day schedule on chart paper from the assessor
Markers and sticky notes for changing the schedule
A blank time log sheet for each member
A clock or a phone timer, and a phone or camera for photos
photos: The day's schedule at the start
The schedule after the first interruption card, with the changes shown
The schedule after the last interruption card
A member role-playing a call to the supervisor or customer
checklist: Stayed calm and chose a sensible new priority for their interruption card
Changed the schedule clearly so everyone could follow it
Told the supervisor or customer about the change politely, early and with a new time
Did not drop safety checks or breaks to catch up
Kept an honest and accurate time log
Added at least one useful improvement to the review sheet
Worked co-operatively and kept to the time of each round
safety: In every decision, keep safety checks in place; never choose to skip them to save time
Keep the role-play area clear of bags and cables
Speak respectfully in the role plays; no shouting or rude words
Take the planned break during the session
